name: Muḥibb al-Dīn Abū al-Baqāʾ ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥusayn al-ʿUkbarī
summary: Blind Ḥanbalī scholar of Baghdad whose al-Tibyān fī iʿrāb al-Qurʾān is the most used grammatical analysis of the Qurʾān, and whose al-Lubāb sets out the causes of grammar.
bio: Abū al-Baqāʾ was born in 538/1143, his family from ʿUkbarā on the Tigris, and lost his sight to smallpox as a child. He learnt grammar from Ibn al-Khashshāb and others in Baghdad and law in the Ḥanbalī school, and taught both; the sources say his students read the books to him and he dictated his own.

His al-Tibyān fī iʿrāb al-Qurʾān (also called Imlāʾ mā manna bihi al-Raḥmān) gives the iʿrāb of the difficult words of every sūra and is printed in the margins of many copies of the Qurʾān. Al-Lubāb fī ʿilal al-bināʾ wa-l-iʿrāb explains the reasons behind the rules, and al-Tabyīn sets out the views of Basra and Kufa on disputed questions. He died in Baghdad in 616/1219.
